screens.title: Agentless Automation and When to Use Ansible
screens.narratorSegment: Network engineers often start with scripts that log in and run CLI commands. Tools like Netmiko provide scriptable, procedural control: you write the exact steps the session must perform. This is powerful for device-unique tasks but becomes hard to scale when you manage many devices with different models and software. Ansible provides a higher-level, declarative model. Rather than scripting keystrokes, you declare the desired state and let a module determine the necessary changes. For example, instead of scripting how to enter interface configuration mode and type commands, you declare that an interface should have a particular description and be enabled. Ansible modules then check the current state and only change what’s needed. A common misconception is that Ansible removes the need to understand device CLI; in reality, you still need to know device behaviors to pick the right module and parameters. Use Ansible when you want repeatable, auditable, and idempotent changes across many devices; prefer scripts for one-off or highly device-specific procedures. As you plan adoption, ask whether a task is about enforcing desired state or performing a one-time diagnostic, and choose the appropriate tool.

Procedural Scripts (e.g., Netmiko)
Scripts log into devices and perform explicit CLI steps in sequence. They give granular control, useful for unique device fixes or when a module does not exist.
Misconception
Scripts always scale well — they don’t. Procedural code is harder to audit and can produce side effects if repeated without careful checks.
Ansible (Declarative & Idempotent)
Declare desired state. Modules compare current and desired configurations and apply only needed changes. This is safer across many devices and supports dry-run checks.
Practical Example
Declare VLANs with cisco.ios.ios_vlans and run ansible-playbook --check first to preview changes.

screens.title: Ansible Architecture: Control Node, Inventory, Modules, Playbooks
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible's architecture is intentionally simple and maps well to network operations. The control node is the machine where you install Ansible and run playbooks; it acts as the central point of automation. Managed nodes are the devices or servers you want to configure. The inventory file lists managed nodes, often grouped by role such as cisco_routers or cisco_switches and can carry host-specific variables. Modules are the units that perform work — for networking you use modules like cisco. ios. ios_vlans and cisco. ios. ios_interfaces which encapsulate logic to check and apply device configuration. Playbooks are YAML files that sequence tasks and target host groups from the inventory. A common mistake is mislabeling ansible_network_os or forgetting to set connection to network_cli, causing modules to fail. Another practical note: gather_facts is often unnecessary for network devices and can be disabled to speed execution. Together these components let you declare desired state and run changes from a central control node while inventory and modules ensure the correct devices and actions are used. What would you put in your inventory for a small access layer deployment?

screens.title: Idempotency and Declarative Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: Idempotency is the property that running the same operation multiple times produces the same outcome as running it once. In network automation this is critical: you want a playbook to be safe to run repeatedly without causing duplicate entries, unexpected additional configuration, or disruptive toggles. Ansible achieves idempotency through its modules. A module inspects the device’s current state, compares it to the declared desired state in your playbook, and executes only the changes required to reach that state. For example, when you declare a VLAN with cisco. ios. ios_vlans, the module will create the VLAN if missing or leave it alone if it already matches the desired name and ID. A common misconception is that idempotency guarantees no transient side effects; in practice modules must be written to check correctly and some edge cases require careful parameter selection. Always validate by running ansible-playbook --check to preview changes, then run again to confirm subsequent runs report OK instead of changed. A practical closing question: after running a VLAN playbook once and then again, what task outputs do you expect to see?

keyIdea.text: Modules compare current vs desired state so repeated playbook runs do not create unintended changes.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Idempotency
Definition & Why It Matters
Idempotency ensures repeated playbook runs result in a stable, predictable device state. It prevents duplicate resources and minimizes risk in production environments.
  • • Modules inspect current state before making changes.
  • • Declarative playbooks state what you want, not how to get it.
  • • Use --check to preview and confirm idempotent behavior.
Concrete Example
When a VLAN 10 already exists with the correct name, cisco.ios.ios_vlans with state: merged will report OK on subsequent runs rather than changed.
Common Pitfall
If a module parameter is omitted or modules are written without checks, repeated runs can still cause changes. Choose modules and parameters carefully.

screens.title: Inventory Files — INI Example
screens.narratorSegment: Inventories tell Ansible which devices to manage and how to connect to them. The INI format is straightforward and well-suited to small to medium device lists. You define groups like cisco_routers and cisco_switches and include host-specific connection variables such as ansible_host, ansible_user, ansible_password, and ansible_network_os. For security, avoid plaintext passwords in inventory; prefer environment variables or Ansible Vault. The example inventory demonstrates grouping and variables for Cisco IOS devices. Practice: place two switches in a cisco_switches group, add ansible_network_os=ios so network modules select the correct platform, then run ansible -i inventory. ini --list-hosts cisco_switches to verify targeting. A common mistake is setting ansible_network_os incorrectly or leaving out the connection type; this leads to modules not being found or permission errors. How would you modify the inventory to add a test router that uses a different username? Inventory Files — INI Example means group devices and attach connection variables; keep passwords out of plaintext by using env vars or vault.. In practical terms, how to list cisco routers and switches with connection variables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Define hosts, connection, become settings, and tasks. Use --check to preview and state: merged for non-destructive updates.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › VLAN Playbook
configure_vlans.yml
---
- name: Configure VLANs on Cisco Switches
  hosts: cisco_switches
  gather_facts: false
  connection: network_cli

  vars:
    ansible_become: true
    ansible_become_method: enable
    ansible_become_password: "{{ lookup('env', 'ANSIBLE_ENABLE_PASS') }}"

  tasks:
    - name: Ensure VLANs exist and are configured
      cisco.ios.ios_vlans:
        config:
          - vlan_id: 10
            name: "DATA_VLAN"
          - vlan_id: 20
            name: "VOICE_VLAN"
          - vlan_id: 30
            name: "MGMT_VLAN"
        state: merged
Run & Verify
  1. 1. Export ANSIBLE_ENABLE_PASS as an environment variable.
  2. 2. Run ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini configure_vlans.yml --check to preview.
  3. 3. If results are expected, run without --check to apply and then inspect device with show vlan brief.
Safety Note
Use state: replaced only when you intend to enforce an exact VLAN set and remove unlisted VLANs.

screens.title: Runbook: Safe Execution and Dry Runs
screens.narratorSegment: Applying changes to network devices requires a predictable, repeatable runbook. Start by preparing inventory and playbook files and ensure you can SSH from the control node to a test device. Next, set any sensitive values as environment variables rather than leaving them in inventory. Always run ansible-playbook with --check to perform a dry run; this previews what would change without altering device state. Review the output for tasks marked changed versus ok. If the dry run matches your intent, run the playbook without --check during a maintenance window if needed. After applying, verify by logging into a device and running show commands to confirm the intended configuration. Finally, run the playbook a second time; expected idempotent tasks should now report OK rather than changed. A common error is missing ansible_become or ansible_become_method which causes permission denied errors when trying to make configuration changes. Following this runbook reduces risk and makes changes auditable and repeatable. content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Safe Execution
Recommended Steps
1. Prepare
Inventory and playbook ready; ensure network reachability from control node.
2. Secure Secrets
Use env vars or Vault for enable passwords; do not store plaintext credentials.
3. Dry Run
Run ansible-playbook --check to preview changes without applying them.
4. Apply & Verify
Run playbook, then confirm on-device with show commands and re-run to verify idempotency.
Common Mistake
Forgetting ansible_become or specifying the wrong connection plugin will cause permission or module errors. Always check connection and become settings first.

screens.title: Connection Methods and Privilege Escalation
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible supports multiple connection methods. For classic CLI interaction over SSH, use connection: network_cli. This plugin handles sending CLI commands and interacting with privilege levels on devices. For devices offering an A P I, such as RESTCONF or NETCONF, connection plugins like httpapi or netconf may be appropriate. In Cisco IOS XE environments where you rely on SSH CLI, network_cli is the right choice. Privilege escalation is handled by ansible_become and ansible_become_method; setting ansible_become: true and ansible_become_method: enable tells Ansible to enter enable mode before running configuration commands. A common misconception is that ansible_become alone is enough; you must also provide the enable password, typically via ansible_become_password. The recommended secure pattern is to read this password from an environment variable so it doesn’t appear in inventory or playbooks. For module selection, also ensure ansible_network_os is set correctly so Ansible picks the right network modules for Cisco platforms. screens.title: Common Ansible Network Modules
screens.narratorSegment: Ansible includes many modules tuned for network platforms. For Cisco IOS devices, cisco. ios. ios_vlans manages VLAN creation and attributes, and cisco. ios. ios_interfaces manages interface state and properties. There is also cisco. ios. ios_config for sending configuration snippets and saving configurations. The advantage of using these specific modules is they are designed to be idempotent and to understand network device constructs, unlike generic command modules that send raw CLI. Use ios_vlans when you need to add or reconcile VLANs declaratively and choose state: merged to add or update without deleting others, or state: replaced when you intend to enforce an exact VLAN set. Module 8 › Chapter 8.5 › Configure Interfaces
inventory.ini (example)
[cisco_routers]
my_router ansible_host=YOUR_DEVICE_IP ansible_user=YOUR_USERNAME ansible_password=YOUR_SSH_PASSWORD ansible_network_os=ios
configure_interfaces.yml (template)
---
- name: Configure Interfaces on Cisco IOS XE Router
  hosts: cisco_routers
  gather_facts: false
  connection: network_cli

  vars:
    ansible_become: true
    ansible_become_method: enable
    ansible_become_password: "{{ lookup('env', 'ANSIBLE_ENABLE_PASS') }}"

  tasks:
    - name: Configure GigabitEthernet1/0/1
      cisco.ios.ios_interfaces:
        config:
          - name: GigabitEthernet1/0/1
            description: "Ansible Configured Interface 1"
            enabled: true
        state: merged

    - name: Save configuration
      cisco.ios.ios_config:
        save_when: always

screens.title: Troubleshooting and Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: When a playbook fails or behaves unexpectedly, methodical troubleshooting saves time. First, confirm connectivity: SSH from the control node to the device with the same credentials specified in inventory. If that fails, fix underlying network or credential issues before debugging Ansible. Second, verify inventory variables: a wrong ansible_network_os or misspelled host group will make modules unavailable or target the wrong hosts. Third, check privilege settings: missing ansible_become or incorrect become_method leads to permission denied when applying configurations. Fourth, run ansible-playbook with -vvv to see detailed output and understand where the module fails. When changes are not applied or produce unexpected config, run --check to preview differences, and inspect the module parameters to ensure they match device semantics. Finally, remember that some modules behave differently between OS versions; test in a lab environment before wide deployment. A practical debugging checklist reduces outages and makes problem reports reproducible for collaboration. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why Ansible is a powerful choice for network automation and how it changes the way you manage Cisco IOS XE devices. Ansible is agentless and communicates over SSH or APIs, which means you don’t install additional software on network devices. That makes it easier to scale from a few routers to many switches while keeping device access simple and auditable. We’ll walk through the architecture: control node, managed nodes, inventory, modules, and playbooks. You will see concrete examples of an inventory file and two playbooks: one for VLANs and one for interface configuration. I’ll explain idempotency — why running the same playbook repeatedly should be safe — and common mistakes like forgetting privilege escalation or using the wrong network OS setting. By the end of this chapter you’ll be able to create a basic inventory, write a declarative playbook using cisco. ios modules, run a dry run to preview changes, and understand how to use environment variables for sensitive data. Think about a routine change you make today on one device — imagine applying that same change reliably across dozens of devices with a single, repeatable playbook. How would that shift your daily workflow?

These objectives show the practical skills you will develop. First, you will explain Ansible's core architecture: what a control node is, how managed nodes are listed in an inventory, what modules do, and why playbooks express desired state. Understanding the architecture helps you design where automation runs and how devices are grouped. Second, you will understand idempotency: why declarative modules check current state and only apply changes when needed. This reduces risk and avoids repeated side effects. Third, you will be able to create and run basic playbooks against Cisco IOS XE devices using connection: network_cli and the proper privilege escalation settings. That means you can automate VLANs and interface configuration safely. Fourth, you will learn to define inventory files to manage multiple devices and to use secure approaches for sensitive data, such as environment variables or Ansible Vault. Each objective includes a short mnemonic to help retention and a milestone marker so you know when you’re ready to apply the skill in the lab.

This second objectives screen focuses on how you practice and verify each skill. For architecture, build a mental map: control node runs playbooks, inventory groups devices, and modules perform work. A practical check is to draw your own network and label which hosts go into which groups. For idempotency, practice by running a playbook twice: the first run may show changes, the second should report OK for unchanged tasks. That demonstrates safe automation. For playbooks, create small YAML files that target a test lab device, use gather_facts: false to speed runs, and always start with --check to preview changes. Finally, for inventories and secrets, practice moving passwords into environment variables and test a login using the same variables. Each practice task reduces risk in production and gives you a repeatable milestone to verify competence.

Network engineers often start with scripts that log in and run CLI commands. Tools like Netmiko provide scriptable, procedural control: you write the exact steps the session must perform. This is powerful for device-unique tasks but becomes hard to scale when you manage many devices with different models and software. Ansible provides a higher-level, declarative model. Rather than scripting keystrokes, you declare the desired state and let a module determine the necessary changes. For example, instead of scripting how to enter interface configuration mode and type commands, you declare that an interface should have a particular description and be enabled. Ansible modules then check the current state and only change what’s needed. A common misconception is that Ansible removes the need to understand device CLI; in reality, you still need to know device behaviors to pick the right module and parameters. Use Ansible when you want repeatable, auditable, and idempotent changes across many devices; prefer scripts for one-off or highly device-specific procedures. As you plan adoption, ask whether a task is about enforcing desired state or performing a one-time diagnostic, and choose the appropriate tool.

Ansible's architecture is intentionally simple and maps well to network operations. The control node is the machine where you install Ansible and run playbooks; it acts as the central point of automation. Managed nodes are the devices or servers you want to configure. The inventory file lists managed nodes, often grouped by role such as cisco_routers or cisco_switches and can carry host-specific variables. Modules are the units that perform work — for networking you use modules like cisco. ios. ios_vlans and cisco. ios. ios_interfaces which encapsulate logic to check and apply device configuration. Playbooks are YAML files that sequence tasks and target host groups from the inventory. A common mistake is mislabeling ansible_network_os or forgetting to set connection to network_cli, causing modules to fail. Another practical note: gather_facts is often unnecessary for network devices and can be disabled to speed execution. Together these components let you declare desired state and run changes from a central control node while inventory and modules ensure the correct devices and actions are used. What would you put in your inventory for a small access layer deployment?

Idempotency is the property that running the same operation multiple times produces the same outcome as running it once. In network automation this is critical: you want a playbook to be safe to run repeatedly without causing duplicate entries, unexpected additional configuration, or disruptive toggles. Ansible achieves idempotency through its modules. A module inspects the device’s current state, compares it to the declared desired state in your playbook, and executes only the changes required to reach that state. For example, when you declare a VLAN with cisco. ios. ios_vlans, the module will create the VLAN if missing or leave it alone if it already matches the desired name and ID. A common misconception is that idempotency guarantees no transient side effects; in practice modules must be written to check correctly and some edge cases require careful parameter selection. Always validate by running ansible-playbook --check to preview changes, then run again to confirm subsequent runs report OK instead of changed. A practical closing question: after running a VLAN playbook once and then again, what task outputs do you expect to see?

Inventories tell Ansible which devices to manage and how to connect to them. The INI format is straightforward and well-suited to small to medium device lists. You define groups like cisco_routers and cisco_switches and include host-specific connection variables such as ansible_host, ansible_user, ansible_password, and ansible_network_os. When a playbook fails or behaves unexpectedly, methodical troubleshooting saves time. First, confirm connectivity: SSH from the control node to the device with the same credentials specified in inventory. If that fails, fix underlying network or credential issues before debugging Ansible. Second, verify inventory variables: a wrong ansible_network_os or misspelled host group will make modules unavailable or target the wrong hosts. Third, check privilege settings: missing ansible_become or incorrect become_method leads to permission denied when applying configurations. Fourth, run ansible-playbook with -vvv to see detailed output and understand where the module fails. When changes are not applied or produce unexpected config, run --check to preview differences, and inspect the module parameters to ensure they match device semantics. Finally, remember that some modules behave differently between OS versions; test in a lab environment before wide deployment.
